heat_spreader.title: Integrated Heat Spreader (IHS)
heat_spreader.description: A nickel-plated copper lid soldered over the silicon, with a stepped retention flange that socket latches grip and a visible silicone seal bead where it meets the package substrate.
heat_spreader.function: Spreads heat from the small die surfaces across a much larger, flat cooling plane so an air or liquid cooler can remove it; mechanically protects the fragile silicon beneath.
heat_spreader.importance: The IHS is the entire thermal and mounting interface of the processor: its flatness and finish decide how well cooler contact transfers heat, and its stepped edge is what the motherboard socket holds onto.
facts: The visible seam between lid and substrate is filled with adhesive sealant during manufacturing.
The blank rectangular field on this reference lid is where a vendor would laser-mark model data - kept empty for brand neutrality.
Delidding (removing the IHS) instantly voids warranties because the dies underneath have no other protection.

thermal_interface.title: Thermal Interface Material (TIM)
thermal_interface.description: A thin metallic-looking layer bridging the gap between the die surfaces and the inside of the heat spreader. This reference shows a solder-like slab; real packages ship indium solder, paste, or polymer depending on product tier.
thermal_interface.function: Fills microscopic air gaps between silicon and lid. Air is a terrible conductor, so even a hairline void would insulate the die and spike temperatures.
thermal_interface.importance: TIM quality sets the ceiling on cooling performance: better interface materials mean lower operating temperatures at the same fan speed and noise level.
facts: Indium solder TIMs conduct heat several times better than silicone pastes.
Some processors let users replace the stock interface with liquid metal for a few extra degrees.
The layer is thinner than a millimeter yet carries hundreds of watts of heat flow in gaming workloads.

compute_die.title: Compute Die
compute_die.description: The primary silicon tile containing the CPU cores and cache. The etched partitions on this brand-neutral representation suggest functional blocks - cores, interconnect, memory subsystems - without copying any vendor floorplan.
compute_die.function: Executes instructions: fetches, decodes and runs billions of operations per second across its cores, exchanging results through on-die interconnect and shared cache.
compute_die.importance: This is 'the processor' in the everyday sense - the piece whose architecture generation largely determines system responsiveness and performance per watt.
facts: A modern compute die packs tens of billions of transistors onto roughly a square centimeter.
Features are printed far smaller than a virus; ultraviolet lithography at these scales is one of humanity's most precise manufacturing processes.
Chiplet designs like this two-tile layout let vendors mix and match silicon process technologies for cost and yield.

io_die.title: I/O Controller Die
io_die.description: The secondary silicon tile handling input/output: memory controller channels, PCIe root complex, and display links. Layout here is a generic educational representation.
io_die.function: Translates between the fast internal world of the compute die and the outside: DRAM timing, expansion card lanes, USB and storage controllers all hang off this tile's fabric.
io_die.importance: Splitting I/O onto its own die lets the compute tile shrink to the most advanced process available, while I/O circuitry stays on a cheaper, more mature node.
facts: Memory support (DDR5 speeds, channel count) is fixed by the I/O die, not the compute die.
PCIe lane assignments you see in motherboard manuals originate from this tile.
Because I/O circuits scale poorly to new nodes, keeping them separate saves cost on the whole package.

substrate.title: Package Substrate
substrate.description: A multi-layer fiberglass-resin board, 1.2 mm thick in this reference, that carries etched copper wiring between the tiny die solder balls and the much coarser land-grid pads below.
substrate.function: Fans out thousands of nanometer-scale die connections into the millimeter-scale grid the motherboard socket can physically mate with, while distributing power and impedance-managing high-speed signals.
substrate.importance: Without the substrate there is no way to connect something as small as a die to something as large as a motherboard - it is the electrical translator of the whole package.
facts: Package substrates are made by the same industry as motherboard PCBs but with far finer traces.
The gold dot near the corner (Pin 1) tells the assembler which way round the chip goes.
Signal paths on the substrate are length-matched so data arrives in step across wide memory buses.

smd_capacitors.title: Decoupling Capacitors
smd_capacitors.description: A bank of 24 multilayer ceramic chip capacitors (0402 size class) seated in a recessed pocket on the package underside - each a two-tone ceramic body with metallic end terminals.
smd_capacitors.function: Act as tiny local reservoirs of charge. When cores switch on in nanoseconds, these caps deliver current before power can arrive from the motherboard voltage regulators.
smd_capacitors.importance: Modern CPUs demand sudden hundred-amp current steps; without local decoupling the supply voltage would sag and crash the chip mid-computation.
facts: Placing them inside the underside cavity puts the capacitance millimeters from the dies that need it.
A single 0402 MLCC contains hundreds of alternating ceramic and metal layers stacked like a mille-feuille.
They are soldered reflow-style: paste dots melt in an oven and surface tension self-aligns each part.

land_grid.title: Land Grid Array (LGA) Contacts
land_grid.description: A dense field of flat gold-plated contact pads arranged in dual banks around the central capacitor cavity - roughly thirteen hundred pads on this reference, at a 0.8 mm pitch.
land_grid.function: Presses against the spring pins of a motherboard socket to carry power, ground, and every data signal between processor and board. No pins on the CPU itself - the pins live in the socket.
land_grid.importance: LGA moved fragility from chip to socket: a bent pad is rarer and less fatal than the bent pins of older pin-grid packages, and denser grids became possible.
facts: Gold plating over nickel prevents oxidation and guarantees contact reliability over thousands of installations.
The gap down the middle of the field is not wasted space - it is the protected cavity holding the decoupling capacitors.
Socket spring pins press up through protective film peel-away; touching the pads with fingers risks corrosion over time.

keying_features.title: Keying & Pin 1 Index
keying_features.description: Asymmetric orientation features: an oversized chamfered corner, gold index triangles on both faces beside that corner, and semicircular alignment notches on one flank only.
keying_features.function: Makes it physically impossible to seat the processor rotated the wrong way - every keying feature must line up with its socket counterpart before the package can sit flush.
keying_features.importance: Power and ground are not symmetric. A wrongly rotated CPU would short supply rails; the keying system turns a destructive mistake into a mechanical non-fit.
facts: Pin 1 convention dates back to early DIP chips and still governs every chip package today.
The gold triangle sits at the Pin 1 corner on both sides of this reference package.
Socket lever force only lines up when the keyed corners match - if it resists, orientation is wrong, never force it.
